newsitem.title: USA: USDA-- survey shows wheat belt free of karnal bunt.
newsitem.headline: USDA-- survey shows wheat belt free of karnal bunt.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department Friday said the results of its nationwide survey so far show the U.S. wheat belt is free of the fungus Karnal bunt.

"Current results of the national survey demonstrate that the vast majority of the United States, including the wheat belt, is free of Karnal bunt," Dr. Charles Schwalbe, associate deputy administrator at USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said in a statement.

On Thursday, state agriculture officials said a grain sample taken from a farm bin in Giles County, Tennessee, tested positive for the fungus and samples from seven other counties were believed to be positive.
The news triggered fears karnal bunt might surface in other growing areas and pushed wheat futures prices down.
Last month, USDA reported there had been three positive samples from wheat in grain and on-farm storage in Alabama.
The department said the disease has not yet been traced to any specific fields in either state and that USDA and state officials were collecting additional samples for testing.

"Where we have found positive samples, we have immediately gone in with intensified surveying and traceback investigations to determine the extent of any possible Karnal bunt infestation and its origin," Schwalbe said.

USDA said it would, in conjunction with officials in Alabama and Tennessee, continue to take those administrative and regulatory actions necessary to conduct the full range of appropriate containment and eradication measures.
The department began the nationwide survey for karnal bunt early last summer after parts of California, Arizona, Texas and New Mexico were quarantined because of the fungus.
USDA said so far more than 10,000 samples have been processed with only 12 testing positive for Tilletia indica spores, the smut fungus that can cause karnal bunt.
The first positive sample was found in California in June, but subsequent tests proved negative. The remaining detections have occured in Alabama and Tennessee, USDA said.

Karnal bunt, also called Stinking Smut, makes wheat smell bad and reduces yields and quality. Many nations refuse to accept wheat that contains the fungus. USDA persuaded customers to continue to buy U.S. grain by issuing documents to prove the wheat did not come from an infected area.
